craft_claim: Nostalgia has a widely shared prototypical core (past-oriented, social, self-relevant, bittersweet) but no uniform voice: local lexicons weight the mixture differently - Japanese natsukashii foregrounds gratitude, Portuguese saudade carries its own time-structure, furusato can harden into politics. The card must not assert a universal nostalgic idiom.

supporting_evidence.note: Samples agreed on the rank-order of 35 nostalgia features and rated previously identified central features as more prototypical everywhere - a shared core. But cluster analyses revealed subtle variation among country groups, and all except the African country samples manifested the same factor structure: shared, not identical.

Saudade's prototypical object is something good from the past, yet it can also target the future (saudades do futuro); it is overwhelming, long-lasting, built on ambiguous thoughts of separation from a beloved person or place, and positively evaluated - a longing whose time-structure and social meaning exceed the English word.
Prototype analysis of how laypersons in Portugal conceptualize saudade documents a locally structured emotion concept rather than a translation of Anglo 'nostalgia'.

Natsukashii derives from the verb natsuku — holding something close until fondness grows — and indicates joy and gratitude for the past rather than a desire to return to it; the article's expert sources describe it as a bittersweet but positively framed reminiscence confirming shared togetherness.

supporting_evidence.location: International Journal of Politics, Culture, and Society 1(4):494-518
supporting_evidence.note: The Japanese case shows a culture's nostalgia vocabulary can be institutionally steered (furusato-zukuri), so the local weighting is not only linguistic but political.

A classical Sanskrit lyric of sustained separation-longing, carried across distance by a messenger - demonstrating an Indian literary practice of longing-at-a-distance more than a millennium before the European word 'nostalgia' existed.

scope: Cross-cultural warrant and its limits; feeds card sections on cross-cultural examples and boundaries.
exceptions: The repository holds no verified source mapping this tone onto a codified Indian rasa; that mapping is recorded as evidence-incomplete (see dossier section E) rather than asserted.
Shared core features support family-resemblance claims only; no sample warrants claiming one universal nostalgic voice.
